topics.title: Scientific investigations & practical skills

notes.heading: How do you distinguish variables?
notes.body: The independent variable is deliberately changed; the dependent variable is measured; controlled variables are held constant. A fair comparison changes one tested factor at a time.

notes.heading: What makes a useful hypothesis?
notes.body: State a testable predicted relationship, ideally with a biological reason. A conclusion must answer the aim using recorded evidence, rather than simply repeating the hypothesis.

notes.heading: How do you improve reliability and validity?
notes.body: Repeat measurements and calculate appropriate summaries to improve reliability. Control confounding factors, use suitable equipment and a comparison/control where appropriate to support validity.

topics.formula: Aim → hypothesis → variables → method → results → conclusion

practice.question: A learner tests how temperature affects amylase activity. Name the independent, dependent and two controlled variables.
practice.answer: Independent: temperature. Dependent: reaction rate or time to a defined endpoint. Controls: pH and enzyme concentration (also substrate concentration/volume where appropriate).

practice.question: Three repeat reaction times are 40 s, 42 s and 38 s. Calculate the mean and explain why repeats help.
practice.answer: Mean = (40 + 42 + 38)/3 = 40 s. Repeats help reveal random variation and anomalous results, making the estimate of typical performance more reliable.

practice.question: A learner tests how light intensity affects the rate of photosynthesis. State the independent variable, one measurable dependent variable and two controls.
practice.answer: Independent: light intensity. Dependent: a suitable measure such as oxygen volume produced per minute. Controls could include temperature and carbon-dioxide availability, as well as plant species and size.

practice.question: Four repeated measurements are 12, 14, 13 and 13 units. Find the mean.
practice.answer: Mean = (12 + 14 + 13 + 13)/4 = 52/4 = 13 units. Repeats provide evidence of variation as well as a central estimate.

practice.question: Explain why repeating an experiment does not automatically remove systematic error.
practice.answer: A systematic error affects measurements in a consistent direction, such as a miscalibrated instrument. Repetition may reproduce the same bias; calibration or a corrected method is needed to address it.

practice.question: Write a testable hypothesis for an investigation of how temperature affects enzyme activity over a range below the enzyme’s optimum.
practice.answer: Example: Over the tested range below the optimum, increasing temperature will increase enzyme reaction rate because particles move more rapidly and form successful enzyme-substrate interactions more frequently.

topics.subject: sports
topics.title: Bones, muscles & movement

notes.heading: What does the skeleton do?
notes.body: The skeleton supports and protects the body, provides muscle attachment sites and acts as a lever system. Bones store minerals such as calcium and phosphorus; marrow produces blood cells.

notes.heading: How do antagonistic muscles work?
notes.body: Muscles generate pulling forces. For a particular movement the agonist produces the main action and the antagonist opposes or controls it. Their roles change when movement reverses.

notes.heading: What are contraction types?
notes.body: Isometric contraction develops tension with no overall muscle-length change. Concentric contraction shortens an active muscle; eccentric contraction lengthens an active muscle while controlling a load.

topics.formula: Muscle force → tendon → bone → joint movement

practice.question: During a controlled biceps curl upwards, identify the main agonist and contraction type.
practice.answer: The biceps brachii is a main elbow-flexion agonist and contracts concentrically as it shortens. The triceps acts as an antagonist.

practice.question: A learner holds a squat still. Name the contraction type and explain it.
practice.answer: The muscles maintaining the position act mainly isometrically. They produce tension without a visible change in overall muscle length or joint position.

practice.question: Name the three main bones of the arm and forearm, and identify which is in the upper arm.
practice.answer: The humerus is the upper-arm bone. The radius and ulna are the two forearm bones.

practice.question: During knee extension, identify the main agonist muscle group and an antagonistic group.
practice.answer: The quadriceps are the main knee-extension agonists. The hamstrings are an antagonistic knee-flexor group. Roles depend on the particular movement being analysed.

practice.question: A person slowly lowers a dumbbell from a flexed elbow. Describe the biceps contraction.
practice.answer: The biceps remains active while lengthening to control the lowering movement, so it contracts eccentrically rather than simply switching off.

practice.question: Give two protective functions of the skeleton, naming a structure and the organ it protects.
practice.answer: The skull protects the brain. The rib cage helps protect the heart and lungs. Other correct structure-organ examples can also be accepted.

topics.subject: sports
topics.title: Energy systems & exercise

notes.heading: How does the ATP-PC system work?
notes.body: Stored ATP and phosphocreatine provide very rapid energy for brief maximal efforts. Capacity is limited, and recovery between efforts helps replenish phosphocreatine stores.

notes.heading: How do glycolytic and aerobic systems differ?
notes.body: Anaerobic glycolysis supplies ATP rapidly from carbohydrate without direct oxygen use. Aerobic metabolism uses oxygen and can sustain ATP production from carbohydrate and fat over longer periods.

notes.heading: Do the systems switch on separately?
notes.body: All energy systems contribute together. Their relative contribution changes with intensity, duration and training. Use sporting examples to justify the dominant contribution rather than claiming exclusive use.

practice.question: Which energy system has a major role in a single maximal 5-second sprint, and why?
practice.answer: The ATP-PC system has a major role because it supplies ATP very quickly for a brief maximal effort. Other systems also contribute.

practice.question: Why is aerobic fitness useful in a match containing repeated sprints?
practice.answer: Aerobic metabolism supports activity between sprints and recovery, including phosphocreatine restoration. It helps the athlete sustain repeated efforts across the match.

practice.question: Compare the dominant energy contribution in a single maximal jump with that in a steady 30-minute run.
practice.answer: A single maximal jump relies heavily on the ATP-PC system because ATP is needed very rapidly for a brief effort. A steady 30-minute run has a major aerobic contribution. All systems overlap rather than operating exclusively.

practice.question: Why do short recovery periods between repeated maximal sprints affect the next sprint?
practice.answer: Phosphocreatine stores may not fully replenish, so the rapid ATP-PC contribution can be reduced. Other energy pathways contribute more, and fatigue may lower the athlete’s ability to repeat the same output.

practice.question: Name the molecule used directly to supply energy for muscle contraction and explain why energy systems must continually regenerate it.
practice.answer: ATP supplies energy directly through its breakdown. Stored ATP is limited, so metabolic pathways continually regenerate ATP from ADP to sustain muscle activity.

practice.question: Why is it inaccurate to say that aerobic metabolism begins only after anaerobic metabolism stops?
practice.answer: The pathways contribute simultaneously. Intensity and duration change their relative contributions; they are not separate switches that turn on only when another system stops.

topics.subject: sports
topics.title: Levers & anatomical planes

notes.heading: What are the parts of a lever?
notes.body: A lever is a rigid structure rotating around a fulcrum. Effort is the applied force and load is the resistance. The effort and load arms are perpendicular moment-arm distances from the pivot to force lines.

notes.heading: How are lever classes organised?
notes.body: First class has the fulcrum in the middle; second class has the load in the middle; third class has effort in the middle. Third-class levers often favour speed and range over force advantage.

notes.heading: Which movements occur in each plane?
notes.body: Sagittal: flexion and extension. Frontal: abduction and adduction. Transverse: rotation. Name the joint and movement, and distinguish the movement plane from the axis perpendicular to it.

practice.question: In a lever, effort lies between the fulcrum and the load. Name the class and give a body example.
practice.answer: It is a third-class lever. In elbow flexion, the elbow is the fulcrum, the biceps applies effort near the elbow and the load is farther along the forearm/hand.

practice.question: A 30 N force acts at a perpendicular distance of 0.2 m from a pivot. Find the torque.
practice.answer: Torque = 30 × 0.2 = 6 N·m. The perpendicular distance to the force line, rather than any arbitrary bone length, must be used.

practice.question: In a lever, the load is between the fulcrum and effort. Identify the class and a human-body example.
practice.answer: This is a second-class lever. Rising onto the toes is a common example: the ball of the foot is the fulcrum, body weight is the load, and calf-muscle force through the Achilles tendon supplies effort.

practice.question: A force of 80 N acts with a perpendicular moment arm of 0.15 m. Calculate the torque.
practice.answer: Torque = force × perpendicular moment arm = 80 × 0.15 = 12 N·m.

practice.question: Identify the main anatomical plane of elbow flexion, shoulder abduction and trunk rotation.
practice.answer: Elbow flexion occurs in the sagittal plane; shoulder abduction in the frontal plane; trunk rotation in the transverse plane.

practice.question: For a balanced lever, a 40 N load acts 0.3 m from the pivot. What effort is required with a perpendicular moment arm of 0.6 m?
practice.answer: Balance torques: effort × 0.6 = 40 × 0.3 = 12 N·m. Effort = 12/0.6 = 20 N, assuming these are the only relevant torques.

topics.subject: sports
topics.title: Nutrition & exercise fuel

notes.heading: What do macronutrients supply?
notes.body: Carbohydrate and protein each supply about 4 kcal/g; fat supplies about 9 kcal/g. Carbohydrate is an important exercise fuel; protein supports growth and repair; fat also supports membranes, insulation and vitamin absorption.

notes.heading: What does glycaemic index compare?
notes.body: GI compares the blood-glucose response to equal amounts of available carbohydrate from different foods. It is affected by food processing and meal context. A carbohydrate-free food is not meaningfully assigned a low GI.

notes.heading: How should you evaluate a diet claim?
notes.body: Ask what evidence supports it, whether the study population matches the claim and whether a source is selling something. School questions about a diet are an opportunity to evaluate evidence, not a personal meal prescription.

topics.formula: Energy ≈ 4 × carbohydrate g + 4 × protein g + 9 × fat g

practice.question: A snack contains 20 g carbohydrate, 5 g protein and 4 g fat. Estimate energy in kcal.
Why is it misleading to describe a carbohydrate-free food as low GI?
practice.answer: GI is measured using a portion containing a standard amount of available carbohydrate. A food with essentially none cannot be compared on that basis, so its GI is generally not applicable.

practice.question: Estimate the energy in a food portion containing 30 g carbohydrate, 10 g protein and 6 g fat. Use 4, 4 and 9 kcal/g respectively.
Distinguish a small calorie from a kilocalorie and convert 250 kcal to small calories.
practice.answer: A kilocalorie equals 1 000 small calories. Therefore 250 kcal = 250 000 cal. Food energy labelled Calories commonly refers to kilocalories.

practice.question: State two functions of dietary fat other than supplying energy.
practice.answer: Fat provides components used in cell membranes and supports absorption of fat-soluble vitamins. It also contributes to insulation and cushioning. These are general biological roles, not a personal diet prescription.

practice.question: A sports-diet article uses one athlete’s success as proof that its diet works for everyone. Give two reasons to question the claim.
practice.answer: A single anecdote cannot establish a general effect, and other influences such as training, genetics and total energy intake may explain the success. A stronger claim needs suitable comparative evidence from relevant populations.

cards.front: What do macronutrients supply?
cards.back: Carbohydrate and protein each supply about 4 kcal/g; fat supplies about 9 kcal/g. Carbohydrate is an important exercise fuel; protein supports growth and repair; fat also supports membranes, insulation and vitamin absorption.

cards.front: What does glycaemic index compare?
cards.back: GI compares the blood-glucose response to equal amounts of available carbohydrate from different foods. It is affected by food processing and meal context. A carbohydrate-free food is not meaningfully assigned a low GI.

topics.subject: sports
topics.title: Heart, lungs & aerobic fitness

notes.heading: What is cardiac output?
notes.body: Cardiac output is the volume pumped by a ventricle per minute. It equals heart rate multiplied by stroke volume. Keep mL and L consistent when calculating.

notes.heading: What is VO₂ max?
notes.body: VO₂ max is the maximum rate of oxygen consumption during intense exercise, often expressed as mL/kg/min. It reflects the integrated ability to deliver and use oxygen, not simply lung size.

notes.heading: How does training affect endurance?
notes.body: Endurance training can increase stroke volume, capillary density and mitochondrial capacity, and lower resting heart rate. Adaptations depend on the training programme and the individual.

topics.formula: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume

practice.question: Heart rate is 150 beats/min and stroke volume is 120 mL/beat. Find cardiac output in L/min.
practice.answer: Q = 150 × 120 = 18 000 mL/min. Divide by 1 000: Q = 18 L/min.

practice.question: Why do thin alveolar walls and many surrounding capillaries support gas exchange?
practice.answer: Thin walls reduce diffusion distance. The capillary network supplies a large exchange area and helps maintain oxygen and carbon-dioxide concentration gradients.

practice.question: An athlete has cardiac output 24 L/min and heart rate 160 beats/min. Calculate stroke volume in mL/beat.
practice.answer: Stroke volume = cardiac output/heart rate = 24/160 = 0.15 L/beat. Multiply by 1 000: 150 mL/beat.

practice.question: At rest, heart rate is 60 beats/min and stroke volume 80 mL/beat. Calculate cardiac output in L/min.
practice.answer: Q = HR × SV = 60 × 80 = 4 800 mL/min = 4.8 L/min.

practice.question: Explain why oxygen transport depends on both the cardiovascular and respiratory systems.
practice.answer: The respiratory system ventilates the lungs and provides gas-exchange surfaces. The cardiovascular system carries oxygen in blood to working tissues. Good gas exchange alone cannot deliver oxygen without circulation.

practice.question: Distinguish an increase in breathing rate during exercise from an increase in mitochondrial capacity after training.
practice.answer: A rise in breathing rate during a bout of exercise is an acute response. Greater mitochondrial capacity developed through repeated appropriate training is a chronic adaptation that can support aerobic ATP production.

topics.subject: sports
topics.title: Arousal, psychology & motor skills

notes.heading: What is the inverted-U model?
notes.body: Performance may improve as arousal rises toward an optimum and then fall as arousal becomes excessive. The optimum varies with the task, skill level and individual; it is a model rather than a universal law.

notes.heading: How do skill demands differ?
notes.body: Fine skills require precise small-muscle control; gross skills use larger muscle groups. Complex tasks often need greater attentional control. Do not assume every athlete has the same optimum arousal.

notes.heading: How can an athlete regulate arousal?
notes.body: Breathing routines, imagery and attention cues can help manage arousal. Match a strategy to the athlete and task, and explain how it could support concentration or readiness.

topics.formula: Low arousal → optimum zone → excessive arousal

practice.question: Use the inverted-U model to explain why too much arousal can hurt a precision task.
practice.answer: Arousal above the athlete’s optimum can increase tension and disrupt attention and fine control. This may reduce accuracy in a precision task such as putting.

practice.question: Give two ways an athlete could reduce excessive pre-match arousal.
practice.answer: Controlled breathing can help regulate physiological activation. A familiar attention routine or calming imagery can redirect focus toward useful task cues.

practice.question: Use the inverted-U model to explain why an athlete who is too relaxed might perform poorly.
practice.answer: Arousal below the athlete’s optimum may reduce alertness, readiness or effort. An appropriate increase could improve performance toward the optimum, but excessive arousal may then impair it.

practice.question: Classify precision dart throwing and a powerful whole-body jump as mainly fine or gross motor skills.
practice.answer: Precision dart throwing depends strongly on fine motor control and accuracy. A powerful jump depends mainly on gross motor coordination and large muscle groups, although both tasks involve several control processes.

practice.question: Two athletes perform the same event but prefer different pre-competition routines. Does the inverted-U model require them to have the same optimal arousal?
practice.answer: No. Optimal arousal can depend on the individual, experience and task demands. The model does not establish one identical level or routine for every athlete.

practice.question: Explain how a short attention cue could help an athlete who is distracted by worries during a skill.
practice.answer: A relevant cue, such as focusing on the target or a movement step, can redirect attention toward controllable task information. The explanation should connect the cue to the specific skill rather than assume all distraction will vanish.

topics.subject: sports
topics.title: Training adaptations & evidence-based essays

notes.heading: How do training principles guide progress?
notes.body: Specificity means adaptations match the training demand. Progressive overload gradually increases that demand. Recovery allows adaptation; excessive load without recovery can impair performance.

notes.heading: Which adaptations are relevant?
notes.body: Resistance training can increase strength and muscle size; endurance training can increase aerobic capacity and fatigue resistance. Separate immediate exercise responses from adaptations developed over weeks or months.

notes.heading: How do you evaluate performance limits?
notes.body: Use evidence about physiology, training, technology and participation. Consider both biological constraints and changes that allow progress. Distinguish fair technological improvements from prohibited practices without assuming a source is neutral.

practice.question: Distinguish an acute response to running from a long-term endurance adaptation.
practice.answer: A raised heart rate during a run is an acute response. An increased stroke volume after months of appropriate endurance training is a chronic adaptation.

practice.question: Give one supported argument on each side of whether athletic records can continue improving.
practice.answer: For improvement: better training methods, technology and wider participation can improve performance. For limits: human physiology places constraints on oxygen delivery, force production and recovery. A conclusion should weigh the evidence for the specific sport.

practice.question: Explain progressive overload using a strength-training example without prescribing a personal programme.
practice.answer: Progressive overload means gradually increasing the training demand as adaptation occurs. For example, a suitable programme may progressively raise resistance or work volume, while allowing recovery and maintaining appropriate technique.

practice.question: Why does a training programme need specificity?
practice.answer: The body adapts to the demands imposed. Training should therefore reflect relevant movements, muscle groups and energy demands; adaptations from one type of training do not transfer equally to every sport.

practice.question: Distinguish a response from an adaptation using two cardiovascular examples.
practice.answer: An increased heart rate during one exercise session is a response. A lower resting heart rate associated with sustained endurance training can be an adaptation. The timescale and repeated stimulus distinguish them.

practice.question: An essay source says new equipment caused a sporting record. What additional evidence would help assess that claim?
practice.answer: Compare performance with and without the equipment under similar conditions, considering training, athlete ability, rules and measurement methods. A record occurring after a new design appeared is not enough by itself to prove the equipment caused it.
